On reading plain pages

This page wears almost no styling. It leans on the browser's own defaults: a serif body face, headings that step down in size, list markers, a little space between blocks, and the familiar underlined link. The point is to test the simplest case there is. If a reader can follow running prose here, on a page that asks the browser for nothing fancy, then the harder pages have somewhere solid to stand. If the words fall apart here, they fall apart everywhere.

Most of the web's text lives in pages much like this one. A title, a few paragraphs, a list of points, the odd quotation, and a link out to somewhere else. The dressing changes from site to site, but the bones rarely do. A single column of words, read top to bottom, is still how we carry an idea from one mind to another. Everything else is decoration laid over that plain frame.

Why the floor matters

When we talk about the floor of legibility, we mean the lowest bar a page can clear and still be read in comfort. It is the page with one column, a sensible measure, and type that is neither too small nor crammed against the edge of the window. Constrain the body to a readable width and let the default font do its work, and the result is calm and easy on the eye.

A long line of text is tiring to read, because the eye has to travel a great distance to find the start of the next line, and sometimes it lands on the wrong one. A narrow measure fixes this. Forty or so characters to a line is a comfortable target for a reader, give or take, and that is why this body is held to a modest width rather than running the full breadth of the screen.

None of this needs a framework or a grid. It needs restraint. The browser already knows how to set a paragraph, mark a list, and quote a passage. Trust it, give it a little room, and stand back. The handful of things to remember are short:

  • Keep one column of running prose.
  • Hold the line length to a readable measure.
  • Set a base size large enough to read without squinting.
  • Leave honest space between the blocks.
  • Let the default font carry the words.

Each of those is a small thing on its own. Together they make the difference between a page that invites reading and a page that fights it. A reader should never have to work to find where a sentence begins or ends.

The best interface for text is text, set plainly, with room to breathe. Everything we add after that should earn its place.

You are looking at original prose, written for this corpus and released under the Blue Oak Model Licence. It carries no tracking, no script, and no fonts pulled from a far-off server. The whole thing is one file. That makes it a fair baseline: whatever a renderer does with this page, it is doing with the browser's plain typography and nothing else. For more on the spirit of plain pages, you might follow this link to further reading, though here it simply jumps to the end.

There is a quiet pleasure in a page that does only what it must. It loads at once. It reads the same on a phone, a laptop, or a terminal. It asks nothing of the reader but attention, and it gives the words back cleanly. That is the floor we are measuring against, and it is a good floor to build on.
